context:
Your gripe: CI runs far too often for how you merge. Your note on the first ask: every option gives up a lot while you are not yet sure merges don't cause regressions, or that the tests pin anything that matters. So option (e) below is new: it earns that trust first, then cuts runs in steps, each step only when a measured bar is met.
Measured: about 16,800 CI minutes a week (Oct 27). Full runs since Oct 25: 21 green, 17 red, 6 cancelled (checked 11:58 CDT, gates workflow); many reds were time caps, not breaks. A batch run takes 26 to 36 minutes. Not measured yet: how often a merge broke something that a later fix had to repair. The options doc has the first four options in full.
home: roadmap step c95; options doc linked below

options.gain: A proven pattern from your own repo.
options.how: Quick checks on each branch, full suite on main, no nightly run.
options.label: q_max's shape
options.lose: Still about 14,300 minutes a week, a small saving.

options.gain: About 8,200 minutes a week, roughly half.
options.how: The batch PR's run is the only full run; main doesn't re-run it.
options.label: No run on main after a merge
options.lose: Nothing re-checks main after a merge, so a break that slips through shows up in the next batch.

options.gain: About 2,400 minutes a week, the biggest cut. This is the 'milestone-style' CI you described.
options.how: A batch is cut at about 4 waiting lanes or 3 hours, and the full suite runs at milestones the build advisor names.
options.label: (b), plus fewer, larger batches and full runs at milestones
options.lose: Breaks are found later and cover more lanes at once. It only works once the full run is trustworthy.

options.gain: What large teams use: safest ordering, few surprises.
options.how: GitHub's merge queue tests each group before it lands, then a batched full run checks main.
options.label: The industry standard: a merge queue plus a batched full run after landing
options.lose: About 9,000 to 10,000 minutes a week, and more setup.

options.gain: You cut CI only when the numbers say merges are safe and the tests mean something, and you see those numbers each week.
options.how: Step 1, now: make the full run trustworthy (split or re-cap the jobs that time out, so red means broken), and measure test value: a mutation check on the guards and hooks shows which tests catch a planted bug and which pin nothing; tests that pin nothing get fixed or deleted. Also count merges that a later fix had to repair. Step 1 costs today's CI (about 16,800 a week) plus three or four build lanes. Step 2, once the full run is green on 9 of its last 10 runs and no merge needed a repair for a week: stop the re-run on main, as in (b), about 8,200 a week. Step 3, after two more such weeks: milestone runs, as in (c), about 2,400 a week. A missed bar sends it back one step.
options.label: Trust first, then cut in steps
options.lose: The big saving comes weeks later, not now. Step 1 adds lane work before any minutes are saved.

owner: The c95 thread (CI at milestones), then the build advisor
ref: c95 part 2 (CI runs at milestones, not on every merge)
title: Which CI rule should claude-settings adopt, so CI runs far less often?
why: It answers your worry directly: each cut waits for a measured bar, and the test-value work is useful whichever CI rule wins.
